extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics and teleology); readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for judging when natural objects can be regarded as purposive or as "natural purposes" (organised beings). Distinguishes internal vs. external purposiveness, sets criteria for organisation/self‑organization, and states the regulative teleological maxims for reflective judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual purposiveness (objective but formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual purposiveness is objective (not merely subjective like aesthetic purposiveness) but only formal: it can be conceived as purposiveness in general without assuming any definite purpose or invoking teleology. Examples include mathematical forms (properties of the circle, parabola, ellipse) whose purposiveness is cognised a priori and strengthens Understanding and Imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe such purposiveness as implying a real external purpose; treat it as an a priori unity of rules and concepts that renders certain forms 'available' for many possible designs. The satisfaction is intellectual (relative perfection, elegance of demonstration) rather than aesthetic. Anti-pattern: attributing empirical teleology to purely intellectual/formal regularities (e.g., treating a geometric property as evidence of nature's final causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative (external) purposiveness / utility
rubrics_metrics.description: External purposiveness (utility or mere advantage) is empirical and relative: something may be useful as a means to other beings (e.g., rivers depositing earth for plant growth, sand enabling pine forests) but this does not make it an objective natural purpose in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat external purposive relations hypothetically and contingently; they may suggest but do not justify absolute teleological judgements. Example usages: rivers, tides, sand deposits, or species used by humans. Anti-pattern: inferring that the existence of such utility proves nature's purposive design or final ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: thing only possible as a purpose (contingency of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing is judged to be only possible as a (natural) purpose if its form is not explicable by mere natural/mechanical laws but requires concepts of Reason to account for its empirical causality; its form's contingency under mechanical laws affords ground for regarding its causality as due to Reason (a will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to distinguish artefacts (produced by rational causes) and products that seem beyond mechanical explanation. Example: finding a regular hexagon in the sand would suggest an artefact rather than a natural product. Beware of over-attributing purposiveness when mechanical explanations may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: a thing as both cause and effect of itself (self‑organising/generative character)
rubrics_metrics.description: To regard a natural product as a natural purpose, it must be (in a double sense) both cause and effect of itself: generically self-producing (species reproducing species), individually self-producing (growth distinctive from mechanical increase), and parts that generate and reciprocally support each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the object exhibits generative self-perpetuation, growth from incorporated materials transformed into novel specific form, and reciprocal dependence among parts (e.g., buds, leaves, twigs). These features indicate self-organisation that mechanical causality alone cannot explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised being criterion (parts as reciprocally end and means)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised product of nature is one in which every part is reciprocally purpose (end) and means: each part exists for the sake of the others and the whole, and the parts are mutually cause and effect of each other's form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defining principle/definition for calling something an organised natural being. Use it as a maxim for teleological judgement: nothing in such a creature is vain. Distinguish organised beings from machines (watches): machines have parts that serve ends but do not produce or replace other parts; organisms self-organise, repair, and produce formative powers beyond mere motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of judging internal purposiveness (teleological maxim: 'nothing is vain')
rubrics_metrics.description: For reflective judgement about internal purposiveness, adopt the maxim that in organised creatures nothing is vain and nothing happens by chance — a regulative, a priori maxim guiding observation and the investigation of natural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this maxim as a methodological guide when studying organisms' structure and function, but recognize it as regulative (not constitutive): it orders inquiry and expectation without itself proving an external teleological cause. It justifies treating features as organs and searching for functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of teleological judgement of nature as system of purposes (regulative idea of collective nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflective judgement may adopt the Idea of nature as a system in accordance with purposes — a regulative principle that expects nothing in nature to be wholly purposeless ('everything in the world is some way good for something'). This guides investigation by subordinating mechanical explanations to a teleological heuristic without negating mechanical causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle only regulatively: it is a maxim for reflective judgement to explore natural phenomena through final causes where productive, but it does not establish that nature is literally designed or that every external purposive relation is an objective natural purpose. Avoid conflating regulative teleology with proof of a supersensible final purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: internal natural perfection vs. aesthetic beauty / intellectual beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate 'internal natural perfection' (objective perfection in organised beings, tied to their being possible only as natural purposes) from aesthetic beauty (reflection upon external aspect) and from intellectual 'beauty' (relative perfection of mathematical demonstrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call mathematical or demonstrative satisfaction 'beauty' in the full aesthetic sense; rather call demonstrations 'beautiful' or 'elegant' insofar as they strengthen Understanding and Imagination a priori. Reserve 'internal natural perfection' for organised beings whose form implies purposiveness and gives objective satisfaction to judgement.
